title: Finesse: An Agile Design Framework for Pairing-based Cryptography via Software/Hardware Co-Design
problem: Pairing-based cryptography (PBC) accelerators require frequent re-engineering as security demands grow and pairing curve parameters evolve, but existing designs are either highly customized (inflexible) or flexible but low-performance, with no framework automating the algorithm-to-hardware translation across diverse pairing curves. The complex interdependency among algorithm choices, finite-field operator variants, and hardware configurations makes design-space exploration intractable manually.
motivation: Evolving cryptographic attacks force migration to larger bit-width pairing curves (e.g., BN254 to BLS24-509), which 2-order-of-magnitude slower than standard signatures, creating an urgent need for an agile framework that cuts re-engineering cycles from months to minutes.
method: Finesse uses a three-layer design: an intermediate representation (shared notation) for math operations on finite and extension fields, a RISC-style instruction set that executes multiple instructions per cycle (VLIW extension), and a customizable hardware pipeline model. A specialized compiler optimizes data flow, schedules instructions using issue-slot affinity (aligning long arithmetic operations with short linear ones to prevent conflicts), allocates registers, and generates executable code. A cycle-accurate simulator measures real performance and feeds results back to both the compiler and the hardware design tools (EDA toolchain) for joint optimization. The hardware implements four core arithmetic operations (mmul, madd, mlin, minv) in a multi-core SIMT (single instruction executing on multiple cores with different data) architecture with shared instruction memory, on both 40nm ASIC and Virtex-7 FPGA.
key_novelty: The innovation is issue-slot affinity scheduling, which partitions the pipeline's instruction slots into periodic intervals and aligns long modular-multiplication operations with short linear operations to eliminate write-back conflicts, combined with a co-design feedback loop between the compiler and hardware synthesis tools (EDA) that jointly optimizes any pairing curve implementation.
contributions: Finesse agile design framework spanning algorithm IR to hardware RTL for arbitrary pairing curves with compilation in minutes
Three-layer abstraction system (IR, ISA, hardware model) decoupling algorithm variants from hardware implementation
Issue-slot affinity scheduling optimization that improves IPC from ~0.19 to ~0.87-0.97 across BN and BLS curve families
34x throughput and 6.2x area efficiency improvement over prior flexible frameworks; 3x throughput and 3.2x area efficiency over state-of-the-art fixed ASIC designs

metrics.area: 1.77 mm2 (1-core, 40nm); 8.00 mm2 (8-core, 40nm); 12.09 kops/mm2 vs 1.39 kops/mm2 for prior ASIC at 65nm equiv.
metrics.ppa: 34x throughput, 6.2x slice efficiency vs FlexiPair; 3x throughput, 3.2x area efficiency vs SOTA ASIC
metrics.other: Compilation time: 8.0s (BN254) to 53.1s (BLS24-509); IPC improved from 0.19 to 0.87-0.97

baselines: Prior state-of-the-art ASIC pairing accelerator (65nm FDSOI, 250 MHz)
limitations: Design-space exploration currently uses exhaustive search over operator variant combinations, which may not scale to the full design space for very complex future curves.
primary_theme: Agile compiler-driven co-design framework for pairing-based cryptography accelerators
